chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Campus memories with Willard: Les Brown, Student Union, Dick Bock
summary: They compare memories of Los Angeles City College, jazz on campus and instructors.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: And you were there during that year?
Yes, in fact Bob Fox was promoting Jazz Calendar Concerts on campus. Red Calendar played on campus, Eric played on campus, in fact Bob Fox introduced me to Eric.
Well, were you there when Les Brown came and played?
I don't remember, so I may have been. I worked --

Well this was the year that they made the tune, I Got My Love to Keep me Warm and Jimmy Zito played this beautiful solo on. And they had the band played in something like the Green Room or Auditorium or something. Isn't there something like a reading room next to a food counter. See the food counter was right in back of the band room. And there was a room just before you got to the food counter. Just off of Vermont.
Oh, yeah, the music room was --
Where the street car turned --
That was on Monroe. Streetcar turned off of Vermont on to Monroe.
All right, well as soon as it turned, the first --
Oh you mean, the Student Union?
Yeah.
The Student Union?

Yeah. Well that's the -- where they let Les Brown play. But I never got any further than my classrooms. I always wanted to go over to the Broadcasting Room and the Jazz Room and what not but I never made it a -- over there.
The jazz room?
Yeah.
What Jazz Room?
They had a radio --
They had a radio station --
Yeah.
A radio building.

Yeah and then they had a jazz, like a rehearsal group over there. Not organized. You know. And the orchestra was the first thing as the car made a turn on Monroe. That was the orchestra room, right there on the corner and I ran into Don Bagley there and later played with Stan Kenton.
Dick Bock was on campus then, Dick Bock
who started what -- Discovery Records a -- with Albert Marsh. Discovery Records and Pacific Jazz. He wrote the Jazz Column in the Collegian.
Yeah?
And he used to give parties and Dade Marmarisa would and play at the party.

Uh-huh. Well I didn't know anything about that. Well in fact my youngest daughter's mother and her cousin, they always came to school with me. They wanted to play piano. So they would just kill time out on the lawn talking until piano time class was and that was after my harmony and theory class.
And the three of us would get in there and play these dummy keyboards, you know. None of us ended up as a piano player. And spend some time.
Do you remember any of your instructors there?

I think my harmony teacher's name was Scott. I don't remember the piano player's, teacher's name and I don't remember the self-teaching and sight singing teacher's name. It was right across the hall from the harmony and theory. In fact, I was in sort of a maze at that particular time. A dream world, you know.
Were you playing professionally?
Huh?
Were you playing professionally or were you going just to school then?
